concept.name: Order routing
concept.definition: The broker-dealer's decision of where to send a customer order for execution: to a national exchange, an alternative trading system, a market maker/wholesaler, an ECN, or its own inventory. Routing determines the price, speed, and likelihood of execution the customer receives.
concept.intuition: The same order can live very different lives depending on which door the broker sends it through - routing is that choice of door.
concept.mechanics: Brokers route manually (directed orders) or via automated routers; the choice weighs quoted price and depth, fees/rebates, speed, and any compensation such as payment for order flow. SEC Rules 605 and 606 of Regulation NMS force transparency: market centers publish execution-quality statistics and brokers publish quarterly order-routing reports.
concept.failure_modes: Routing optimized for the broker's economics (PFOF, exchange rebates) rather than the customer's execution quality is the structural conflict; disclosure mitigates but does not eliminate it. Static routing tables also degrade when venue liquidity shifts intraday.
concept.misconceptions: Retail customers can often direct their own orders to specific venues, but few do - and 'commission-free' does not mean routing is free of economic incentives. Routing to the exchange showing the best quote is not automatically best execution either.
concept.example: Your broker's router sends your 500-share market buy to a wholesaler that pays for order flow and fills it a tenth of a cent inside the offer, instead of to the exchange posting the NBBO.
